title: Should he teach?
hook: he hesitates; Brahma Sahampati asks him to teach; he sees people like lotuses near the surface (MN 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two merchants: Tapussa and Bhallika, honey-cakes, and the first lay followers. Your line was the first gift. Who did you give a snack to? Day fifty-nine.

Have you ever understood something so deeply that you didn't know how to say it? Maybe you went through something hard, a loss, an illness, a recovery, and came out the other side knowing something. And then someone asked you about it, and you opened your mouth, and it just sounded like a greeting card. Some things don't fit into words very well. The Buddha has found what he was looking for. Now comes a question that's easy to skip past. Should he tell anyone at all? Today, should he teach?
screen: `TOO DEEP FOR WORDS.` → `IT SOUNDED LIKE A GREETING CARD.` → `SHOULD HE TELL ANYONE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this himself. What I've found, he thinks, is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, subtle, beyond mere reasoning. And people love their attachments. They delight in them. For people like that, this would be hard to see. If I taught it, and others didn't understand, that would only be wearying for me. So his mind leans toward doing nothing, toward not teaching. And then, the sutta says, a great god, Brahma Sahampati, realizes what's happening. The world will be lost, he thinks, if the awakened one stays silent. In the time it takes a strong man to stretch out his bent arm, the god leaves his heaven and appears before the Buddha. He kneels, raises his joined hands, and pleads. Let the Blessed One teach. There are beings with only a little dust in their eyes. They're losing out because they haven't heard. Some will understand. So the Buddha looks out over the world, with the eye of an awakened one. And what he sees is a lotus pond. Some lotuses are still deep under the water. Some have grown right up to the surface. And some stand clear above it, untouched by the water. People are like that, he sees: some with much dust in their eyes, some with little, some ready right now. And he decides. Open are the doors to the deathless, he says, for those who have ears. It's a gentle ending to his hesitation. Not everyone is ready. But some are ready, and for them, it's worth it.
screen: `DEEP, SUBTLE, HARD TO SEE.` · `BRAHMA KNEELS AND PLEADS.` · `A LITTLE DUST IN THEIR EYES.` · `LOTUSES AT EVERY DEPTH.` · then, large: `SOME ARE READY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Close your eyes and picture a still pond. Under the surface, green stems reach up from the mud. Pick one lotus bud and watch it. Slowly, slowly, it rises through the dark water, toward the light. It breaks the surface. It stands in the air, drops of water rolling off. Then, petal by petal, it opens. Let the picture move at its own speed. If your mind wanders, return to the pond. The bell holds the time.
Should he teach? The moment the Buddha hesitated, until Brahma Sahampati pleaded and he saw people like lotuses, some ready to rise.
Your line: some are ready. Today, share one thing you've learned with someone who seems open to it, and don't worry about the ones who aren't. Day fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 59 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MAN ON THE ROAD.`

howItsDone: In the Pali telling, Brahma Sahampati's request is the turning point that sets the teaching in motion, and in some traditions a formal request to teach is made to a teacher before a dharma talk, echoing this moment.

match.prompt: what's inside the moment — tap the pairs.
pairs: knelt and asked him to teach
a little dust in their eyes

myth: the Buddha first thought his teaching would be easy to grasp
he found it deep, subtle and hard to see, and his mind leaned toward not teaching.
in the sutta, a god asks the Buddha to teach
Brahma Sahampati kneels and pleads: some have only a little dust in their eyes.
the Buddha saw that everyone was equally ready
he saw lotuses at every depth: some deep, some near the surface, some already above it.

fork.setup: you've found something deep and hard to put into words. a god kneels before you: some will understand. what do you do?
options: stay silent: they won't get it.
look out over the world, and decide to teach.
fork.reveal: he surveys the world and sees people like lotuses at every depth. the doors to the deathless are open, he says, and he decides to teach.

original.note: Pali: lotus (Sanskrit padma), one of the flowers in the Buddha's vision of the pond.

trapdoor: what you thought: of course the Buddha wanted to teach.
what it means: he hesitated, because it was so hard to say. a god's plea and a vision of lotuses changed his mind.

what a scholar hears: MN 26 and SN 6.1 (Brahmayacana Sutta): the Buddha's hesitation, Sahampati's request, the blue, red and white lotuses (uppala, paduma, pundarika), and 'open are the doors to the deathless'.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the hesitation and the request

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the closing line no longer borrows the Gospel phrase 'ears to hear'; it follows MN 26 ('open are the doors to the deathless for those who have ears'). Replaced a myth item that repeated day 57's ('left right after waking'). howItsDone no longer claims what all Buddhists remember.

MN 26 / SN 6.1 paraphrased throughout, including 'open are the doors to the deathless' and 'let those who have ears' (the line about giving up faith, pamuñcantu saddham, is rendered variously and is simplified here). Confirm.
'The time it takes a strong man to stretch out his bent arm' is the canon's stock phrase; confirm paraphrase.
